teaser.text: United Utilities is the water and wastewater utility for North West England: it turns water from the environment into a service at the tap, then collects and treats much of what customers send down the drain. Its business is a regulated regional system, so a pound comes in through recurring charges and goes out through operations, investment and finance.

stock.opening: United Utilities’ weighted price is 1,711.90 GBp in October 2029. The United Utilities case hinges on AMP8 investment becoming delivered assets and returns without debt, penalties or dilution absorbing the benefit.
stock.closing: The full United Utilities memo also covers its business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could United Utilities’ shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The forecast puts the weighted price at 1466.27 GBp in October 2027. Including dividends, that is a 2% return. It reaches 1575.14 GBp in October 2028, equivalent to a 13% return. By October 2029, the weighted price is 1711.90 GBp, giving a 26% return.

The three-year range runs from 1023.09 GBp in the bear case to 2500.13 GBp in the bull case. Today’s price is 1495.00 GBp. The base case has the largest probability at 55%, against 25% for the bear case and 20% for the bull case.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for United Utilities, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case assumes cost pressure, penalties and financing reduce EPS. The bull case assumes more investment is approved, delivered efficiently and supported by better service. FY26 capital spending of £1,492.1m exceeded operating cash of £1,381.9m, while net ODI penalties were about £35m. Those facts justify keeping both downside and execution risk visible.

blocks.heading: How much cash does United Utilities really make?

paragraphs.text: Cash from operations was £1,381.9 million in FY26. The company then spent £1,492.1 million on capital investment. Real free cash flow, after capital spending, lease payments, interest already included in the cash-flow statement and stock-based pay, was negative £117.4 million. It was also negative £76.5 million in FY25.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for United Utilities?

paragraphs.text: Cash flow explains why a profitable utility can still have a negative free-cash-flow yield. UU spent £1,525m on capital expenditure in FY26 and plans about £11.5bn across AMP8. Like renovating a house, the cash leaves today while the assets are expected to create value over many years.

blocks.heading: How much does United Utilities pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The dividend also depends on delivery. UU paid a FY26 dividend of 53.66p per share and intends to grow dividends with CPIH inflation, but FY26 included a net ODI penalty of about £35m. The regulatory return was 13.0% against an AMP8 target of 10–11%. The price must therefore be tested against UU’s past as well as its plan.

Dividends rise with CPIH in the base case, freeze in the bear case and grow slightly faster in the bull case. The base path moves from £0.5554 to £0.5961086 by October 2029. FY26 DPS was £0.5366, and FY27 guidance is £0.5554. The history of annual increases supports the base, but investment spending and funding pressure make a freeze credible.

blocks.heading: Is United Utilities' dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: The pattern is more important than any single year. Free cash flow covered shareholder payments at the start of the period, but payments exceeded it in 2023 and free cash flow became negative thereafter. Dividends were the main shareholder payment, while buybacks remained small and the table shows no acquisitions. Debt issued exceeded debt repaid in the later years, so net debt rose even as cash and short-term investments also increased.

Cash from operations was £1,381.9 million in FY26. The company then spent £1,492.1 million on capital investment. Real free cash flow, after capital spending, lease payments, interest already included in the cash-flow statement and stock-based pay, was negative £117.4 million. It was also negative £76.5 million in FY25.

blocks.heading: What could change United Utilities' dividend?

paragraphs.subsection: 5.5 — How group financing reaches the regulated water business
paragraphs.text: Ring-fencing means the licence protections designed to keep UUW financially and operationally able to provide the service. UUW’s directors certified that it had sufficient resources for at least the next 12 months. Ofwat also expects dividend decisions to reflect service, investment and financial resilience. The group paid £357.6 million in dividends in FY26, but that payment alone does not show that UUW had surplus cash safely available.

blocks.heading: What has United Utilities guided for FY27?

paragraphs.text: Management says investment is on track and expects the regulated asset base to grow strongly. Its return target is a regulatory return, not a guaranteed shareholder profit: it depends on the regulator’s allowance, inflation, service performance and the avoidance of penalties. Ofwat’s allowed return is 4.03% real CPIH for AMP8, before those further effects.

The base case gains support if FY27 revenue approaches management’s £2.7–2.8bn guidance and AMP8 investment continues near plan. It also requires gearing to remain within the 55–65% target and dividends to track inflation.

paragraphs.subsection: 5.5 — How group financing reaches the regulated water business
paragraphs.text: The latest interim comparison shows the same mixture of regulation, accounting and operating conditions. Revenue rose from £1,082.0 million in the six months to September 2024 to £1,309.2 million in the six months to September 2025. Operating income also rose sharply, while the period included the new price settlement, IRE capitalisation and unusually dry conditions that increased resilience costs.

blocks.heading: What should people watch in United Utilities' next results?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is the half-year report due on 12 November 2026. It should show whether revenue, costs, depreciation and investment are developing as management expects. Ofwat’s consultation on the FY26 outcome-delivery adjustment closes on 5 November 2026. Its final determination is due on 15 December.

The separate cost-change decision, expected in December, will show how much of the expansion is allowed and whether conditions apply. Approved allowances, gated funding and directly funded assets should be kept distinct because they carry different levels of certainty.
